steps.title: Austerlitz — command map, 2 December 1805
steps.card: The Battle of Austerlitz French formations are marked in blue and the Allies in amber: on their names, their counters and the ground beneath them, and on the movement arrows. The high ground in the centre is the Pratzen plateau, which this map reads as deciding the battle. Begin (two min) Explore on my own
steps.now: derived on the heights: Allied ≈ 38,700 Friant's division at Raigern since the night (an interval, not a timestamp) Davout and Friant reached Raigern on the night of 1 December: about 115 km from Vienna in under two days in Sokolov, thirty-six leagues in forty-eight hours in Thiers. Davout's reports send the division on from Raigern at 05:00 (his report of 2 December) or between 05:30 and 06:00 (his report of 26 December), Sokolov about six; this map moves it from 05:00. Raigern lies just beyond this corner of the map. 04:00 - 07:00 Dispositions in the dark Napoleon has deliberately given up the Pratzen plateau and left his right, along the lower Goldbach, looking thin enough to invite attack. Weyrother's Allied orders, read out at Krzenowitz after midnight to commanders who largely did not understand them, send four of five columns south-west across the French front. Fog fills the Goldbach valley. Soult's two assault divisions are standing in it, invisible from the heights. c. 01:00 Weyrother reads the dispositions at Allied headquarters, Krzenowitz. Kutuzov reportedly dozes. c. 04:00 The disposition orders the Allied columns to march at seven; Thiébault records reports through the night of the Allied left moving, judged by the noise. Liechtenstein's cavalry, misplaced on the left, must counter-march north across the front of the 4th Column; the Materialien has it ordered off only at dawn. before dawn Napoleon mounted at one in the morning to ride round his posts (the 30th B

acts: The Deception | The Deception, 04:00 to 07:00: Napoleon has given up the plateau and left his right thin. The Allies form to attack it.
The Allied Advance | The Allied Advance, 07:00 to 08:45: Four columns go down into the Goldbach villages. The centre of the Allied position empties behind them.
The Pratzen Strike | The Pratzen Strike, 08:45 to 10:30: Soult climbs out of the fog onto ground the Allies have just left, and holds it against everything sent back.

The Army Divided | The Army Divided, 10:30 to 12:45: With the plateau lost the Allied army is in two halves. The Guard, which Stutterheim calls the reserve of the Allied right, attacks to take it back and is thrown back.
The Collapse | The Collapse, 12:45 to 18:00: The French centre turns south onto the rear of an Allied left that is still attacking westward.

steps.head: On accuracy and uncertainty Tagged in this dossier Imperial Headquarters (France), its army's figure: Not yet checked Imperial Headquarters (France), its army's source: Not yet checked Imperial Headquarters (France), 04:00 - 07:00: As a source tells it (Napoléon Ier (Commission), no. 9534, p. 441; А. И. Михайловский-Данилевский, p. 177; Napoléon Ier (Commission), no. 9535, p. 443) That the height is the Zuran is an identification; no source read names it. Imperial Headquarters (France), 04:00 - 07:00, its objective: This map's reading (by its kind) Positions here are reconstructed from standard accounts of the battle. Village-level locations and the sequence of attacks follow the accounts; the hours are partly dated in the sources read, partly disputed between them, and mostly this map's own, as each move's timing grade, and each event's timing and dispute, say. Exact frontages, the spacing between formations and the precise placement of cavalry reserves are not — a Napoleonic corps occupied a shifting area of ground, not a point. Every formation marker therefore carries a confidence grade. A means the position is documented; B means the sector is documented but the frontage shown is an approximation; C means the position is reconstructed from the narrative and should be treated as indicative only. Strengths are the hardest figures of all. The Allied column organisation split and intermingled regiments, and reputable orders of battle disagree substantially — Dokhturov's I Column is given as anything from 7,750 to 14,200 men. Where sources conflict, the dossier shows a working figure and the range. Terrain relief is exaggerated about 4 times: one map unit is 32 m on the ground, and heights follow a separate vertical scale fitted to surveyed elevations. At true scale the Pratzen plateau reads as a gentle rise, about 115 m from the Goldbach to the Pratzeberg over some 2.5 km. The relief setting cannot be changed while the battle plays, because redrawing the ground can take longer than a frame; the ground switch (Landscape, Paper map, Landscape with counters) can, and a slow frame while it redraws advances the battle clock by at most 1.2 minutes at 1× (4.8 at four times speed). Villages are placed from the Czech municipality register; Turas, which it does not list, at the Czech address register's point for Tuřany, its name in Wolny's topography of 1836; Krug and Bellowitz, which no register read places, are not; summits from terrain-model data. The map keeps its historical frame, which lies about 17 degrees off true north. The compass rose shows true north for the current view. Raigern, Rausnitz and Kowalowitz lie beyond the frame and are shown as markers at its edge. steps.text: On accuracy and uncertainty Positions here are reconstructed from standard accounts of the battle. Village-level locations and the sequence of attacks follow the accounts; the hours are partly dated in the sources read, partly disputed between them, and mostly this map's own, as each move's timing grade, and each event's timing and dispute, say. Exact frontages, the spacing between formations and the precise placement of cavalry reserves are not — a Napoleonic corps occupied a shifting area of ground, not a point. Every formation marker therefore carries a confidence grade. A means the position is documented; B means the sector is documented but the frontage shown is an approximation; C means the position is reconstructed from the narrative and should be treated as indicative only. Strengths are the hardest figures of all. The Allied column organisation split and intermingled regiments, and reputable orders of battle disagree substantially — Dokhturov's I Column is given as anything from 7,750 to 14,200 men. Where sources conflict, the dossier shows a working figure and the range. Terrain relief is exaggerated about 4 times: one map unit is 32 m on the ground, and heights follow a separate vertical scale fitted to surveyed elevations. At true scale the Pratzen plateau reads as a gentle rise, about 115 m from the Goldbach to the Pratzeberg over some 2.5 km. The relief setting cannot be changed while the battle plays, because redrawing the ground can take longer than a frame; the ground switch (Landscape, Paper map, Landscape with counters) can, and a slow frame while it redraws advances the battle clock by at most 1.2 minutes at 1× (4.8 at four times speed). Villages are placed from the Czech municipality register; Turas, which it does not list, at the Czech address register's point for Tuřany, its name in Wolny's topography of 1836; Krug and Bellowitz, which no register read places, are not; summits from terrain-model data. The map keeps its historical frame, which lies about 17 degrees off true north. The compass rose shows true north for the current view. Raigern, Rausnitz and Kowalowitz lie beyond the frame and are shown as markers at its edge. Open questions, left unresolved rather than guessed: the pattern of Russian infantry flags; whether Grenz infantry wore brown in 1805; whether vines stood at Telnitz and at Stare Vinohrady in 1805; the upper bound of the Russian Guard's attack; Bagration's exact line at dawn; whether the Posoritz post house stood in 1805 where the maps of 1826-52 show the post; the positions of Krug and Bellowitz, which no source read fixes; Kologrivov's command on 2 December, which rests on Sokolov alone (Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky and the Chevalier Guard's history have him command the Guard cavalry at Olmütz and on the march, and the Chevalier Guard came up in Maliutin's separate column); when Blasowitz fell; when Napoleon took post on the Zuran; when Bernadotte's corps, Drouet's division with it, crossed the Goldbach; how many guns stood by the chapel of St Anthony, and whose; how many men drowned in the meres; how Suchet's and Caffarelli's divisions were numbered on the day (Suchet's the 3rd of V Corps in both October returns read, Gazan's the 2nd on 26 October; Caffarelli's, under Bisson on 28 October, the 1st of III Corps); the brigade of Gladkov cited from Duffy and Smith, which no source read names; whether Uvarov's regiments were with Liechtenstein's column or had gone to Bagration the evening before; the numbers of Rivaud's and Drouet's divisions in I Corps, which the October returns give differently; and the hours on which the accounts read disagree with each other or with this map's timing: when the columns left the plateau (at 07:00 as the disposition ordered, the I Column at seven in Buxhowden's and Kutuzov's reports and so on the map, half past six for the left wing in Schönhals, between seven and eight in Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky; the II and III Columns at 07:30 in Schönhals, the III at 07:00 in Przybyszewski's report and the II coming down at 08:00 in Buxhowden's; all three from 07:00 on the map), when Kamensky turned his brigade about (no account read gives the hour; at 09:45 in the event, in the 08:45 phase in his brigade's record), when Rapp's counter-charge went in (by about noon in Schönhals, before one by the order of the Bulletin's narrative, about 13:00 in Rapp's and Ségur's memoirs; from 11:15 on the map), when Friant's division left Raigern (at 05:00, or between 05:30 and 06:00, in Davout's two reports, about 06:00 in Sokolov; at 05:00 on the map, with its leading brigade at the Goldbach about 09:00, as in Stutterheim and the Moniteur's remarks of 1806, and Telnitz in French hands at 09:30, then lost again, as in Davout's report), and when Bagration's corps fell back (with Blasowitz's fall on the map, 11:15; after an attack on its left toward noon in Schönhals). The map keeps its timing for Kamensky's turn, Rapp's charge and Bagration's corps. Duffy (1977) and Smith (1998), cited here for strengths, were not read. Kamensky's musketeer regiment is named here as Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky names it, Ryazhsk; the Materialien of 1806 give Ryazan, as this map earlier cited from Duffy, which is kept as the other reading. Two known limits of the terrain model are left as they are rather than reshaped to fit: its stream beds are not downhill at every point (reverse gradients of up to about 10 m within a reach), and from the chapel of St Anthony it does not show the centre of the Satschan pond, although Lejeune has Napoleon at the end on a knoll above Augezd facing the lakes, which this map takes to be the chapel's height. Two figures on the situation line are computed from the plotted reconstruction rather than taken from a source. The holding on the heights is the sum of the strengths of formations whose plotted positions fall inside the plateau outline; because the reconstruction plots formations and not losses, a figure that does not change does not mean the fighting there has stopped. Centre separation is a spatial test, not a historical statistic: it reports whether a French formation stands across the line joining the Allied groups north and south of the plateau. When it stops being reported the geometry no longer holds, which is not the same as the Allied army having reunited. Three layers Historical record What the sources attest: who was there, roughly how many, which villages were attacked and when. Marked as fact in an event's dossier. Reconstruction How this map represents the record: a plotted position, a route between anchors, a frontage. Graded A, B or C for confidence; a formation's dossier names the grade as its position's: documented, estimated or reconstructed. Derived reading What the engine computes from the plot, such as the holding on the heights or the centre-separation test. Never a source figure; the holding on the heights and the centre-separation test are marked derived wherever they are shown. Confidence grades A: Position documented in the sources. B: Sector documented; the frontage shown is an approximation. C: Reconstructed from the narrative — treat as indicative only. On the map each formation's grade is drawn on the ground under it: A as its modelled footprint, crisp; B as a soft frontage, twice the footprint's width and fading at its ends; C as a diffuse zone whose radius is the formation's own frontage. These are drawn sizes, not measured errors: the sources grade a position, they do not give its error. Between two plotted positions a formation is drawn at the weaker grade. Each name and counter also carries its grade's letter. The evidence skeleton (a layer, off at first) draws each formation's plotted positions, the anchors the clock moves between, as small marks by grade (filled: A, ring: B, open ring: C; a tick where the position carries an explicit time), and the lines this reconstruction interpolates between them. The lines are not recorded routes. The ordered routes (a layer, off at first) draw each plan column's line of march, dashed and faint, as the two plans set them out: intentions, not what was marched. A formation's dossier then gives the largest distance of its executed track from its column's route, derived. Basis Order-of-battle figures are this map's working figures, many first taken from Duffy (1977) and Smith (1998), cited and not read; where a formation's note names a source or gives what the sources read, it says so, and a figure without a note is this map's. Narrative of the fight for the Pratzeberg draws on Thiébault's memoirs, with Schönhals and Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky where the statements name them; Duffy (1977), on which it earlier drew, was not read. Figures for the meres: General Suchet's report of 16 December 1805, as Sokolov quotes it (2006, t. II, pp. 70-71, his note 88 citing Alombert and Colin, Paris, 2002, t. 5, p. 297; the French text was not read), has the pond near Augezd drained over five days and 36 Russian guns, 13
